title: What are the @GeneratedValue strategies (IDENTITY, SEQUENCE, TABLE, AUTO, UUID), how does each generate keys, and which should you choose?
shortTitle: IDENTITY vs SEQUENCE vs TABLE vs AUTO vs UUID?

s1_definition.profdef: `@GeneratedValue` tells JPA how to produce primary-key values. `GenerationType.IDENTITY` relies on a database auto-increment column (MySQL `AUTO_INCREMENT`, PostgreSQL `SERIAL`/`IDENTITY`); the id is assigned by the database on INSERT, which means Hibernate CANNOT batch inserts because it needs each row's generated id immediately. `GenerationType.SEQUENCE` uses a database sequence object (`CREATE SEQUENCE`) and lets Hibernate pre-fetch a block of ids via an allocation size, enabling batching; it is the preferred strategy on databases that support sequences (PostgreSQL, Oracle). `GenerationType.TABLE` emulates a sequence using a dedicated key table and row locking — portable but slow, used only when the database lacks sequences. `GenerationType.AUTO` lets the provider pick based on the dialect (modern Hibernate often chooses a sequence). `GenerationType.UUID` (JPA 3.1) or a Hibernate UUID generator produces a 128-bit UUID, letting the application generate the id without any database round trip — great for distributed systems, but a random UUIDv4 as a clustered primary key causes index fragmentation.
s1_definition.analogy: When National Bank of India opens a new account it needs a unique number. IDENTITY is like a ticket machine at the branch that stamps the next number only when you reach the counter (one at a time). SEQUENCE is like being handed a strip of fifty pre-printed numbers to use at your own desk (fast, batchable). TABLE is like a shared logbook where everyone writes the last-used number under lock (portable but creates a queue). AUTO lets the bank's system pick the method for you. UUID is like generating a globally-unique reference yourself without asking the central registry at all.
s1_definition.oneliner: IDENTITY uses DB auto-increment (no batching); SEQUENCE pre-fetches id blocks (preferred, batchable); TABLE emulates sequences portably but slowly; AUTO lets the provider choose; UUID is app-generated and distribution-friendly but random UUIDv4 fragments clustered indexes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@GeneratedValue` tells JPA how to produce primary-key values. `GenerationType.IDENTITY` relies on a database auto-increment column (MySQL `AUTO_INCREMENT`, PostgreSQL `SERIAL`/`IDENTITY`); the id is assigned by the database on INSERT, which means Hibernate CANNOT batch inserts because it needs each row's generated id immediately. `GenerationType.SEQUENCE` uses a database sequence object (`CREATE SEQUENCE`) and lets Hibernate pre-fetch a block of ids via an allocation size, enabling batching; it is the preferred strategy on databases that support sequences (PostgreSQL, Oracle). `GenerationType.TABLE` emulates a sequence using a dedicated key table and row locking — portable but slow, used only when the database lacks sequences. `GenerationType.AUTO` lets the provider pick based on the dialect (modern Hibernate often chooses a sequence). `GenerationType.UUID` (JPA 3.1) or a Hibernate UUID generator produces a 128-bit UUID, letting the application generate the id without any database round trip — great for distributed systems, but a random UUIDv4 as a clustered primary key causes index fragmentation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When National Bank of India opens a new account it needs a unique number. IDENTITY is like a ticket machine at the branch that stamps the next number only when you reach the counter (one at a time). SEQUENCE is like being handed a strip of fifty pre-printed numbers to use at your own desk (fast, batchable). TABLE is like a shared logbook where everyone writes the last-used number under lock (portable but creates a queue). AUTO lets the bank's system pick the method for you. UUID is like generating a globally-unique reference yourself without asking the central registry at all.

**One line to remember:** IDENTITY uses DB auto-increment (no batching); SEQUENCE pre-fetches id blocks (preferred, batchable); TABLE emulates sequences portably but slowly; AUTO lets the provider choose; UUID is app-generated and distribution-friendly but random UUIDv4 fragments clustered indexes.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the throughput problem that made us revisit key generation at National Bank of India.

Problem 1 — a nightly import was crawling because of IDENTITY. We import millions of trade rows every night. The trade table used IDENTITY, and because Hibernate cannot batch inserts with IDENTITY, each row was a separate INSERT round trip and the import took hours. This is exactly where SEQUENCE helps: with an allocation size, Hibernate pre-fetches a block of ids and batches the inserts, collapsing many round trips into few.

Problem 2 — a new distributed payments service needed ids before hitting the database. The payments service generates an idempotency reference that must be returned to the caller immediately and must be unique across many instances. This is exactly where a UUID strategy helps: the id is generated in the application without a database round trip and is globally unique.

Problem 3 — the first UUID attempt fragmented the index. The payments table used a random UUIDv4 as its primary key, and write throughput degraded as the table grew because random ids scatter inserts across the B-tree. This is exactly the UUIDv4 fragmentation caveat; the lesson recorded in the project is to use a time-ordered id for the clustered key.

Problem 4 — a legacy module ran on a database without sequences. One older integration used a database that lacked sequence support, so we fell back to the TABLE strategy, accepting its slower, lock-based generation because portability mattered there.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is an `Account` entity using SEQUENCE with an `allocationSize` of 50 for efficient batched inserts. There is a `PaymentRef` entity using the UUID strategy to generate an id in the application. There is a `LegacyRecord` entity using the TABLE strategy to show the portable fallback. The `KeyGenService`, annotated `@Transactional`, saves a batch of accounts (showing the sequence hands out a block) and creates a payment reference (showing the id exists before save). The demo logs how many sequence calls back a batch of inserts and prints the pre-assigned UUID. A test verifies the UUID is non-null before persistence and that the strategies are configured as intended.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a nightly batch creating one hundred accounts, and a single payment reference for a distributed service.

Step 1: `createAccountsBatch(100)` runs in a `@Transactional` method and builds one hundred transient `Account` objects, none of which has an id yet.

Step 2: We call `accountRepo.saveAll(accounts)`. Because the id uses `GenerationType.SEQUENCE` with `allocationSize = 50`, Hibernate calls `SELECT nextval('account_seq')` and receives a value that reserves a block of fifty ids. It assigns those ids to the first fifty accounts in memory without any further database calls, then makes a second sequence call for the next fifty. So one hundred accounts need only about two sequence round trips instead of one hundred.

Step 3: Because the ids were obtained up front, Hibernate can use JDBC batching (`jdbc.batch_size: 50`) and send the INSERTs in batches rather than one at a time. Had the entity used IDENTITY, Hibernate would have been forced to execute each INSERT separately to read back each generated id, and batching would be impossible.

Step 4: `createPayment(5000, "Priya Sharma")` builds a transient `PaymentRef`. Because the id uses `GenerationType.UUID`, the provider generates a 128-bit UUID in the application. The id exists before any database interaction, which is exactly what a distributed service wants when it needs to return a reference immediately or use it as an idempotency key.

Step 5: `paymentRepo.save(ref)` issues a single `INSERT INTO payment_refs (id, amount, payee) VALUES (?, ?, ?)` with the already-known UUID. The note in the result records the senior caution: a random UUIDv4 primary key fragments a clustered index, so a time-ordered id like UUIDv7 or ULID is preferred for the clustered key.

```

2026-10-24 00:40:05 FINE  KeyGenService - SELECT nextval('account_seq') ×2, then batched INSERTs (batch_size=50)
2026-10-24 00:40:05 INFO  KeyGenService - [UUID] Payment ref id generated in app: b1f2c3d4-... (no DB round trip)
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ FIVE @GeneratedValue STRATEGIES ═══

  IDENTITY  → DB auto-increment (SERIAL/AUTO_INCREMENT)
              INSERT → DB assigns id → Hibernate reads it back
              (Caution) cannot batch (one INSERT per row)

  SEQUENCE  → SELECT nextval('account_seq') with allocationSize=50
              one call reserves 50 ids → assign in memory → batch INSERTs
              (Recommended) preferred on PostgreSQL/Oracle

  TABLE     → id_keys row (key_name, next_val) read+increment under LOCK
              portable to any DB, but lock serialises generation (slow)

  AUTO      → provider picks based on dialect (often SEQUENCE on modern Hibernate)

  UUID      → 128-bit id generated in the APP (no DB round trip)
              (Recommended) distributed-system friendly, id known before save
              (Caution) random UUIDv4 as clustered PK → page splits, index bloat
              fix: UUIDv7 / ULID (time-ordered, append-friendly)

  ═══ BATCHING IMPACT (1000 inserts) ═══
  IDENTITY : 1000 individual INSERTs (no batch)        → slow
  SEQUENCE : ~20 sequence calls + batched INSERTs       → fast
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The GeneratedValue annotation tells JPA how to produce primary-key values, and there are five strategies. IDENTITY relies on a database auto-increment column, so the id is assigned during the insert; the important consequence is that Hibernate cannot batch inserts, because it must execute each insert individually to read back the generated id. SEQUENCE uses a database sequence object and, with an allocation size, pre-fetches a block of ids in one call, which keeps batching working and is my default on PostgreSQL and Oracle. TABLE emulates a sequence with a dedicated key table and row locking; it is portable to any database but the lock serialises generation, so it is the slowest and I use it only when the database lacks sequences. AUTO lets the provider pick based on the dialect, which is convenient but I prefer explicit strategies in production. UUID generates a 128-bit id in the application with no database round trip, which is ideal for distributed systems.

In our systems at National Bank of India, the trade and account tables use SEQUENCE with an allocation size so the nightly import batches inserts and finishes quickly instead of making one round trip per row. The distributed payments service uses the UUID strategy so it can generate an idempotency reference in the application and return it to the caller immediately, before any database interaction.

The senior caution I always give is about UUIDs as primary keys. A random UUID version 4 scatters inserts across the B-tree index, causing page splits and index fragmentation, and this is especially damaging on InnoDB where the primary key is the clustered index, so write throughput degrades as the table grows. The fix is a time-ordered identifier such as UUIDv7 or ULID, which stays globally unique but keeps inserts append-friendly. I also keep the sequence allocation size aligned with the actual sequence increment to avoid gaps or collisions, and I accept that surrogate keys may have gaps, which is perfectly fine.

keyPoints: IDENTITY: auto-increment, breaks JDBC batch — INSERT needed for ID
SEQUENCE: pre-allocate IDs, batch-friendly — best performance
TABLE: simulated sequence, portable but lock contention
UUID: app-generated, no DB round-trip, but index fragmentation risk
